newsitem.title: USA: Travelers fret as American Airlines strike looms.
newsitem.headline: Travelers fret as American Airlines strike looms.

text.p: Tens of thousands of air travelers braced for chaos and some suffered St. Valentine's Day heartbreaks on Friday as pilots prepared to shut down American Airlines, the second biggest U.S. carrier.
With a strike deadline set for midnight EST Friday (0500 GMT on Saturday), U.S. airports were jammed as passengers scrambled to rearrange plans and get on flights before the deadline.

"I am terribly worried. I have no other flight to go to and I want to get back to my husband," said Betty Moore, a Californian in her early 20s, as she stood in line for a standby ticket to Sacramento.

Her original flight was scheduled to leave Dallas on Friday night but she feared it would be cancelled because of the looming strike. "I'll sit here in the airport until I can get out of this place. I'm sick of it all."
Close to tears, Moore said she couldn't afford the extra $260 she would need to fly out on another airline.
In the Haitian capital of Port-au-Prince, Natasha Civil, 21, said she could not get to New York to be with her boyfriend. "This has ruined my Valentine's Day. My heart is broken."

Dallas salesman Dan Cummins said he was intent on visiting his girlfriend in Chicago for Valentine's Day but will be in trouble if he gets stranded and misses work on Monday. "My boss is going to be mad as hell if I don't get back on time."
American's management and pilots' union leaders met for a fifth straight day of negotiations in Washington on Friday in a last-ditch effort to cut a new four-year labour contract.

Both sides and a federal mediator said progress was slow and pilots insisted they were determined to strike if no deal was reached by midnight, although talks could continue with the airline shut down.
American is the second largest U.S. airline, accounting for 20 percent of domestic flights and carrying about 200,000 passengers on 2,200 daily flights.
It cancelled almost all of Friday's international flights because it did not want planes stranded abroad. A handful of domestic flights were also cut.

Travel agents said any strike would batter the tourist industry in the Caribbean, which is in its peak winter holiday season, and could cause havoc at American's home base of Dallas-Fort Worth as well as airports in Chicago, Miami, New York and San Juan, Puerto Rico.
But Chris Privett of the American Society of Travel Agents said many passengers had lined up alternatives and would only be delayed or inconvenienced rather than stranded.
Thousands of passengers cut short their vacations to avoid getting caught in a strike.

In Puerto Rico, Danny McDaniel, 43, said he had planned to stay until Saturday but jumped in a car and drove across the island when told there was a seat available for Friday. "The strike messed me up on a surfing contest."

A pilots' strike would cost American's parent company AMR Corp. upwards of $30 million per day and federal government officials said it could cost the U.S. economy between $100 million and $200 million per day.
Most of AMR's 90,000 employees will be placed on unpaid emergency leave if a strike begins. Tens of thousands more could be laid off by tourism firms and the airline's suppliers.
American has said it will try to rebook all stranded passengers on other airlines.

"They have told me they'll get us back, but we have nothing in writing," passenger Phillip McCrory said as he and his wife, Debbie, waited to leave Dallas for their 25th wedding anniversary vacation to Honolulu on Friday.

American Airlines executives, senators and business leaders from around the country have urged President Bill Clinton to push the two sides into binding arbitration, but pilots' union leaders say they do not want Clinton involved and White House officials refused on Friday to discuss any possible intervention.
